title: Long SPCX — Second Qualifying Close Re-Entry (June 22 Binary)
entry: Enter $183–195 on June 23 open IF June 22 US session closes above $185 on above-average volume (>150M shares), confirming the second consecutive qualifying close above the re-entry trigger. Pair with July $165 put as a hedge. Do NOT enter before the June 22 close is confirmed — the two-consecutive-close rule is the entire risk-management framework after the June 18 stop at $174.90. If June 22 closes below $185, the first-qualifying-close count resets and re-entry is suspended until two new consecutive closes above $185 are logged.
stop_loss: $165 daily close (~11.4% below the $186 entry midpoint) — per the briefing re-entry framework established after the June 17 stopped-out position; below this level the float-normalization thesis is structurally compromised and the stock is in a new base-building phase. The July put hedge offsets most of the stop-to-entry loss.
targets: $207 — prior June 15-17 resistance zone before options expiry IV-crush; first profit-take as SPCX reclaims pre-volatility territory; +11.3% from $186 midpoint; take 40% of position
$225 — prior ATH retest at $225.64; MSCI passive float normalization buying completes as 120-day lock expiry approaches for pre-IPO shareholders; +20.9%; take 40%

$252 — blue sky re-rating: Starship orbital cadence confirmed above 10 missions/year, Artemis contract extensions, and SpaceX-Tesla Powerwall + Starlink synergy priced into sum-of-parts model; +35.5%; hold remaining 20%
catalyst: SpaceX (SPCX) IPO'd June 12, 2026 at ~$135 per share, first day close $161 (+19%) on record-breaking $75B raise. The stock rallied to ATH $225.64 before pulling back; a June 17 stop at $174.90 triggered the prior position exit. June 21 logged the first qualifying close above the $185 re-entry trigger ($191.82). June 22 is the binary: a close above $185 on above-average volume confirms the second qualifying close and activates the June 23 re-entry. IG credit ratings (Moody's Baa1, Fitch BBB+, S&P BBB) priced June 22 reduce one of the discount factors that drove the post-IPO selloff. MSCI passive float normalization over the 120-day lock-expiry window is the structural bid that creates a sustained inflow schedule independent of daily sentiment.
thesis:
SpaceX's SPCX trades at the intersection of four premium-valuation drivers that do not exist simultaneously in any other publicly traded company: (1) a launch-cadence monopoly (68%+ of global orbital payload capacity in 2025), (2) a satellite internet subscription business with 6M+ Starlink subscribers generating recurring ARPU of $120/month, (3) an AI-infrastructure edge (Starlink low-latency ground stations as an alternative backhaul to hyperscaler data centers), and (4) a government-contract floor from NASA Artemis, US Space Force, and the $24B SATCOM contract. The sum-of-parts valuation at the $75B IPO was conservative — the Starlink business alone justified $40-50B at 2.5x ARR. Post-IPO institutional float normalization is still early: the 120-day lock expiry for pre-IPO employees creates a passive-index buying program that phases in over the next 60-90 days as MSCI mandates build to their float-adjusted weight.

The re-entry framework is specifically designed to avoid the trap of chasing the stock back into a downtrend. The June 18 stop at $174.90 (long-spcx-post-options-iv-normalization-2026-06-17) was triggered by a combination of elevated implied volatility, the Juneteenth long weekend reducing liquidity, and a modest risk-off tone from the Iran-DXY-FOMC complex. None of those factors invalidated the underlying float-normalization thesis — they created a temporary bid vacuum. The two-consecutive-close rule above $185 filters out single-session noise and confirms that institutional buyers have returned.

The two binary conditions for June 22 both point in the same direction. First, the SPCX June 22 daily range ($172.11-$190.00) confirms the stock is volatile but HOLDING the $185 re-entry level intraday. Second, IG credit ratings now priced in reduce the institutional discount on equity (investment-grade companies trade at lower equity risk premiums than unrated), creating a structural support bid from crossover institutional buyers who require IG credit before taking equity exposure. A June 22 close above $185 at above-average volume would confirm institutional sponsorship returning after the post-IPO digest period.

The counter-party is the SpaceX skeptic who argues: (1) the $75B IPO valuation exceeded sum-of-parts even with the full float build — Starlink ARPU is pressured by competitors and international expansion costs; (2) NASA Artemis contract timing slippage risks (two delays already in 2025) could reduce the government-floor valuation; (3) TSLA's declining market share in EV creates conglomerate-discount risk as Musk allocates attention away from Tesla. These are legitimate risks; the 2% position size and July $165 put hedge are calibrated to the elevated single-name volatility.
bull_case: June 22 closes at $191 on 175M shares (above-average, second qualifying close confirmed). June 23 entry at $189-192. Starship Super Heavy completes orbital mission June 25, driving news coverage that re-ignites retail buying interest. MSCI passive inflow schedule begins June 23 as float-adjusted weight increases to 0.12% of emerging market index by August. SPCX to $225 within 3 weeks; $252 by mid-July on sum-of-parts upgrade.
bear_case: June 22 closes at $183 (below $185 trigger) on below-average volume. Re-entry is suspended. DXY stays above 100.00 into the week; risk-off from PCE June 25 drives a broader tech selloff that drags SPCX to $175-178, threatening the $165 support. The two-qualifying-close count resets and the position is not entered; the open opportunity holds as 'active' pending a new qualifying window.
invalidation: $165 daily close (if entered); OR DXY closes above 101.00 on June 22 US session AND SPX breaks below 7,460 — combined risk-off that removes the float-normalization bid from passive mandates; OR SpaceX files amended S-1 disclosures that reveal material undisclosed liabilities or NASA contract amendments; OR Starship orbital mission fails in a publicly visible way that impairs the launch-monopoly valuation premium
